topic: Unlocking the Geometry of Networks: Planar Graphs and Euler’s Formula
target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Mathematics majors)

outline.topic: Unlocking the Geometry of Networks: Planar Graphs and Euler’s Formula
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Mathematics majors)

sections.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph
sections.content: Define a planar graph as a graph that can be drawn in a 2D plane without edges crossing. Introduce the concept of 'Faces' (the enclosed regions including the infinite outer region).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Spider-Man' web: If he shoots webs that don't cross, it's a planar graph. If they tangle, it's not.

sections.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula
sections.content: Introduce the fundamental theorem: V - E + F = 2 (Vertices - Edges + Faces = 2). Explain that this relationship holds true for any connected planar graph.
sections.example: An animation of a simple triangle (V=3, E=3, F=2) transforming into a square (V=4, E=4, F=2) to show the constant result of 2.

sections.title: The Concept of Duality
sections.content: Explain how to construct a dual graph: Place a dot (vertex) in every face of the original graph, and connect these dots if the faces share an edge.
sections.example: Transforming a 'Cube' skeleton: Representing the 6 faces of a cube as 6 vertices in an octahedron-like dual structure.

sections.title: The Duality Relationship
sections.content: Show how the properties of the dual graph relate to the original: The number of vertices in the dual equals the number of faces in the original (V* = F, E* = E, F* = V).
sections.example: A side-by-side animation of a map (regions) turning into a network of communication towers placed in the center of those regions.

sections.title: Real-world Application & Summary
sections.content: Summarize how these tools allow engineers to optimize circuit board layouts and map coloring problems. Recap: Planar graphs simplify complex systems into solvable geometry.
sections.example: Designing a microchip: Showing how to reroute a 'crossing' wire by using duality to find an empty 'face' to pass through, ensuring no electrical short-circuits occur.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph
lecture_lines: Planar graphs have no crossing edges.
animations: Fade in a simple graph with vertices and crossing-free edges in #FFFFFF.
Highlight vertices with #FF5733 and edges with #33FF57.
Flash the complete graph to emphasize its planar nature.
Change edge colors to #3357FF as they are traced out.
Rotate the entire graph slowly to demonstrate no overlaps.

storyboard.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula
lecture_lines: Vertices minus edges plus faces equals two.
Works for any connected planar graph.
A triangle has three, three, two.
animations: Display Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 in #FFFFFF.
Highlight 'V' in #FF5733, 'E' in #33FF57, and 'F' in #3357FF.
Animate values V=4, E=6, F=4 to confirm the formula.
Flash the equals sign and the constant 2.
Group all elements and move them to a corner of the screen.

storyboard.title: The Concept of Duality
lecture_lines: Place a vertex in each face.
animations: Draw a planar graph in #FFFFFF with centers marked in #FF5733.
Connect centers of faces to form the dual graph in #33FF57.
Highlight the transformation of face to vertex.
Pulse the original graph to show it fading into the background.
Emphasize the dual graph with #33FF57 bolding.

storyboard.title: The Duality Relationship
animations: Show the original graph and dual graph side-by-side.
Draw lines linking original edges and dual edges in #FF5733.
Scale the dual graph to fit within the original's face.
Show the correspondence of V* and F in #3357FF.
Flash both graphs to indicate duality equivalence.

storyboard.title: Real-world Application & Summary
animations: Display a map divided into regions in #FFFFFF.
Overlay the dual graph on the map using #33FF57.
Highlight one dual edge corresponding to a border.
Flash the whole structure to summarize the concept.
Fade everything out, leaving only the formula V - E + F = 2.
